content: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a severe and potentially life-threatening complication of uncontrolled diabetes, primarily seen in individuals with autoimmune type 1 diabetes, though it can also occur in some cases of type 2 diabetes. The standard treatment for DKA involves the administration of regular insulin through intravenous infusion, typically initiated in the emergency department and continued in an intensive care or high-dependency unit setting. However, it remains uncertain whether subcutaneous administration of rapid-acting insulin analogues could serve as an alternative treatment modality for DKA. To evaluate this, researchers conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogues with standard intravenous regular insulin in patients with DKA. The trials included participants of any age or sex with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, as well as pregnant women. The review identified five trials involving a total of 201 participants, with 110 receiving subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogues and 91 receiving intravenous regular insulin. The criteria for diagnosing DKA in these studies were consistent with the American Diabetes Association's definitions for mild or moderate DKA. Most cases of DKA were attributed to poor adherence to diabetes therapy. However, the trials provided limited information on the type of diabetes among participants, and younger individuals, including children, were underrepresented. Four of the trials investigated the effects of the rapid-acting insulin analogue lispro, while one trial examined the effects of aspart. The average hospital stay across the studies ranged from two to seven days. The overall risk of bias in the included trials was unclear in many areas, with a high risk of performance bias specifically for the outcome of time to DKA resolution. No deaths were reported in the included trials. For subcutaneous insulin lispro compared to intravenous regular insulin, there was very low-quality evidence regarding the time to resolution of DKA, with a mean difference of 0.2 hours (95% CI -1.7 to 2.1; P = 0.81) based on data from 90 participants in two trials. In one trial involving children, the time to achieve a blood glucose level of 250 mg/dL was similar between the two treatment groups. For subcutaneous insulin aspart compared to intravenous regular insulin, there was also very low-quality evidence, with a mean difference of -1 hour (95% CI -3.2 to 1.2; P = 0.36) based on 30 participants in one trial. Regarding hypoglycemic episodes, low-quality evidence suggested no significant difference between the two treatment approaches. Among participants treated with insulin lispro, 6 out of 80 experienced hypoglycemic events, compared to 9 out of 76 participants treated with regular insulin (risk ratio [RR] 0.59; 95% CI 0.23 to 1.52; P = 0.28). For insulin aspart, the RR for hypoglycemic episodes was 1.00 (95% CI 0.07 to 14.55; P = 1.0) based on 30 participants in one trial. Socioeconomic outcomes, as measured by the length of hospital stay, showed no significant differences between the two treatment groups. For insulin lispro compared to regular insulin, the mean difference in hospital stay was -0.4 days (95% CI -1 to 0.2; P = 0.22) based on 90 participants in two trials. For insulin aspart compared to regular insulin, the mean difference was 1.1 days (95% CI -3.3 to 1.1; P = 0.32) based on low-quality evidence. Data on morbidity were limited, and no specific adverse events were reported for the comparison of insulin lispro with regular insulin. None of the trials reported on adverse events other than hypoglycemic episodes, nor did they assess patient satisfaction. In conclusion, this review, which primarily included data from adult participants, found no clear advantages or disadvantages when comparing subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogues to intravenous regular insulin for the treatment of mild or moderate DKA. The evidence supporting these findings was predominantly of low to very low quality.
